claims.text: An ML interatomic potential calibrated for defects and thermal disorder will predict electrical conductivity more accurately than conventional analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage will hold for bulk HfNbTaTiZr across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The proposed MLIP can be calibrated to represent intrinsic defects and 1 wt.% oxygen impurities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Finite-temperature molecular dynamics with Monte Carlo updates can explicitly incorporate defect scattering and temperature-induced lattice disorder for this conductivity prediction.
Oxygen impurity clusters and thermally induced lattice disorder mediate scattering events that affect transport.
Explicit simulation of defect interactions and thermal vibrations captures increased scattering events.
Increased scattering caused by defects and thermal vibrations reduces electrical conductivity.
The scattering increase is especially strong in HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Conventional analytical approaches assume perfect crystals and ignore defect-induced scattering.
The MLIP-based predictions will quantitatively match experimental conductivity benchmarks in both temperature regimes.
HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen will have lower conductivity than the pristine material.
The oxygen-containing material will have more temperature-sensitive conductivity than the pristine material.
The MLIP approach will capture low-to-high-temperature crossover behavior better than analytical models.
Defect-free analytical models typically overestimate conductivity because they neglect defect and impurity scattering.
The framework is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
The framework is validated only within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Prediction accuracy may depend on how representative the defect configurations used for MLIP calibration are.
Relevant scattering mechanisms are less understood at extremely low temperatures.
Failure to improve significantly over analytical predictions, or deviations exceeding the acceptable margin in either temperature regime, would falsify the approach.

contradictions.description: The boundary calls the framework 'validated' within the two temperature ranges, while the proposed experiment is framed as the future test that would establish or falsify that validation.

The hypothesis predicts comparative superiority over analytical models, but the example threshold of less than 15% deviation is an absolute-error criterion and does not establish improvement over the baseline. The wording also places this favorable error level inside a condition introduced by 'do not show' improvement.
